questions.question: Which statement best captures bilinearity for a pairing e: G1 × G2 → GT?
options: e(aP, bQ) = e(P, Q)^(ab) for scalars a, b and points P, Q
e(aP, bQ) = a·e(P, Q) + b·e(P, Q) in the target group GT
e(P, Q) = e(Q, P) for all points P, Q (pairings must be symmetric)
e(P, Q) outputs a curve point that you can add using the EC group law
questions.explanation: Bilinearity means the pairing turns scalar multiplication in G1/G2 into exponentiation in GT: e(aP, bQ) = e(P, Q)^(ab).

questions.question: When validating a BLS12-381 point received from the network, which approach is insufficient on its own?
options: Only check that the point is on the curve; on-curve does not imply correct subgroup
Check the point is on the curve and in the prime-order subgroup (or clear cofactor)
Reject the identity point when the protocol requires a nonzero key or signature
Use a standards-based hash-to-curve method for messages instead of ad-hoc mapping
questions.explanation: On-curve checks are necessary but not sufficient on curves with nontrivial cofactors; you must ensure prime-order subgroup membership (or clear cofactor).

questions.question: What does the embedding degree k tell you for a pairing-friendly curve?
options: The extension degree k where GT lives inside F_{p^k}^* for pairing outputs
The number of bits in the base field modulus p that defines the curve equation
The cofactor size for G1 that determines how many points are off the subgroup
The window size used in wNAF scalar multiplication to speed up point multiplication
questions.explanation: k is the smallest extension degree where the r-torsion and r-th roots of unity exist, so the pairing can map into a subgroup of F_{p^k}^*.

questions.question: Why is BN254 commonly used in Ethereum zkSNARK verifiers?
options: Ethereum provides BN254 precompiles for EC ops and pairing checks (EIP-196/197)
BN254 guarantees ~256-bit security in GT, so it is always stronger than BLS12-381
BN254 is the only curve family that supports pairings with embedding degree 12
BN254 eliminates the need for subgroup checks because all points are prime order
questions.explanation: BN254 is popular on Ethereum because precompiles make the pairing and related EC operations efficient on-chain; the choice is largely ecosystem-driven.

questions.question: In many libraries, pairing(P, Q) expects P in G2 and Q in G1. What can go wrong if you swap them?
options: You can get type/curve mismatches or silently compute a meaningless value for the protocol
Nothing; pairings are always symmetric so the result is guaranteed to be identical
It always returns the identity element in GT, so verification still passes safely
The library will hash the inputs into the right groups automatically and continue
questions.explanation: Pairing APIs typically assume specific groups for each argument. Swapping them can throw errors or produce values that do not match the protocol equation.

questions.question: What is cofactor clearing used for in BLS12-381 hash-to-curve?
options: To map an on-curve point into the prime-order subgroup required by the protocol
To compress the point into fewer bytes for network transport and storage
To speed up pairing computation by reducing the embedding degree from 12 to 2
To derive the curve order r from the field modulus p without external parameters
questions.explanation: Hash-to-curve first maps to the curve, then clears the cofactor (or equivalent) so the output is guaranteed to be in the correct prime-order subgroup.

questions.question: Which failure mode can happen if a verifier accepts a BLS public key that is not in the prime-order subgroup?
options: The pairing check can collapse to 1 = 1 for degenerate keys, enabling trivial forgeries
The discrete log problem becomes polynomial time in the base field, breaking all curves
Signatures become longer but remain unforgeable because GT still has order r by design
Only performance degrades; subgroup checks are a speed optimization, not a security rule
questions.explanation: If keys can live in small/cofactor subgroups, pairing equations can become degenerate and accept forged signatures (e.g., identity signatures) unless subgroup rules are enforced.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the security tradeoff between BN254 and BLS12-381 in modern practice?
options: BN254 is fast and common in Ethereum tooling, but GT security is below a 128-bit target
BN254 is always strictly stronger because its r is ~254 bits while BLS12-381 is larger
BLS12-381 is weaker because the larger p makes discrete log in GT easier via NFS attacks
There is no meaningful difference; any curve with k=12 automatically has equal security
questions.explanation: Both curves have similar r sizes, but pairing-target security differs; BN254 is typically treated as ~100-bit in GT, while BLS12-381 targets ~128-bit.
